title: Turkey pan gravy
summary: Roasting-pan drippings and stock simmered with herbs and thickened with a pinch of xanthan gum instead of a flour roux.

ingredients.note: or more stock; plus the drippings left in the turkey roasting pan
ideally homemade from the turkey neck
to taste; drippings from a dry-brined bird are already salty

steps: Pour the drippings from the roasting pan into a heatproof jug and let the fat rise for 5 minutes. Spoon off all but about 2 tablespoons of fat and return the juices to the pan.
Set the pan over medium heat (across two burners if needed) and soften the shallot in the fat for 2 minutes. Add the wine and scrape up the browned bits, then let it bubble until reduced by half.
Add the stock, thyme and sage and simmer 5 minutes. Strain into a small saucepan if you want it smooth.

With the gravy at a simmer, sprinkle the xanthan gum over the surface while whisking hard, a little at a time, so it does not clump. Simmer 1–2 minutes; it thickens as it heats. Add a few more pinches only if it is still thin — too much turns it slippery.
Off the heat, whisk in the cold butter. Taste, then season with salt and pepper.
dairy_free_notes: Dairy-free butter gives the same gloss; without any butter the gravy is a little thinner and less rich but still good.
tips: An immersion blender is the easiest way to disperse xanthan gum without lumps.
Drippings carry very few carbs, but skip any pan juices that have sugar from a sweet glaze.

origin.history: Serving roast meat with a sauce made from its own juices is an old English habit; by the 1700s English cookery books routinely described gravy made from pan juices and stock. The thickened brown gravy that accompanies roast turkey carried over into American cooking and became a fixed part of the Thanksgiving table in the 1800s.
